title: Skyroot Aerospace Makes History as India's First Private Orbital Rocket Puts Six Payloads Into Space
excerpt: The Hyderabad startup's Vikram-1 reached a 450-kilometre orbit on its maiden flight from Sriharikota, marking a turning point for India's private space sector.
body:
• Skyroot Aerospace's Vikram-1 successfully placed six payloads, including two satellites, into a 450-km low-Earth orbit from Sriharikota on July 18 — making it the first Indian private company to achieve orbital launch.
  • The 23-metre rocket, built entirely in India by a team of roughly 1,000 people with over 400 suppliers, exceeded all expectations on its maiden flight.
  • Prime Minister Narendra Modi called the Skyroot founders immediately after the mission, calling it proof of India's self-reliance in space technology.
  • Vikram-1 is the first of three planned developmental missions before entering commercial service in the growing global small-satellite launch market.

A Maiden Flight That Exceeded Every Expectation

India's private space sector reached a defining milestone on Friday when Hyderabad-based Skyroot Aerospace launched Vikram-1, the country's first privately developed orbital rocket, from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre at Sriharikota and successfully placed six payloads into low-Earth orbit.

The 23-metre-tall, 1.7-metre-diameter rocket lifted off from the First Launch Pad at 12:05 p.m. IST as part of Mission Aagaman — Hindi for "arrival." The three-stage solid-fuel vehicle, equipped with a restartable liquid-fuelled Orbit Adjustment Module for precise orbital insertion, delivered its cargo to a 450-kilometre orbit at an inclination of roughly 60 degrees.

"The mission objective was to simply clear the tower. It went all the way up to 450 km orbit, successfully completed all the tasks — something that is way beyond expected in the very first launch."

— Pawan Kumar Goenka, Chairman, IN-SPACe

The payloads included the Solaras S3 satellite from Bengaluru-based Grahaa Space, a robotic arm called Embrace built by Hyderabad's Cosmoserve Space for future space-debris removal, a technology demonstration from German company DCubed, and Skyroot's own SCOPE payload. The mission also carried Cosmic Bloom, an artwork made from lab-grown diamonds by Cosmos Diamonds, and a handwritten postcard from Prime Minister Narendra Modi bearing the words "Vande Mataram."

Modi Hails 'Atmanirbhar' Milestone

Minutes after the mission was declared a success, Prime Minister Modi spoke over the phone with Skyroot CEO Pawan Kumar Chandana and co-founder Naga Bharath Daka. Modi called the launch proof that India can be self-reliant in space, conveying what he described as "grand greetings" and urging the team to push forward with Mission Aagaman.

"Your card has successfully reached orbit. Vande Mataram is in orbit," Chandana told the Prime Minister, referring to the postcard Modi had given the team before launch.

"This is a historic moment not just for Skyroot, for India and also for the entire global space sector. The rocket is 100 percent built by Indians in India," Chandana said after the mission, noting that the achievement represented the work of roughly 1,000 people, contributions from over 400 suppliers, and nearly 3,000 days of development.

The Technology Behind Vikram-1

Built using advanced carbon-composite structures, Vikram-1 is designed to carry up to 350 kg to low-Earth orbit and about 260 kg to Sun-synchronous orbit. Its propulsion systems include 3D-printed engines and high-thrust solid-fuel rocket boosters, all developed in-house by Skyroot.

Many of the vehicle's key technologies — including propulsion, avionics, thermal protection systems and composite structures — were first demonstrated during Skyroot's Vikram-S suborbital mission in November 2022, which made history as the first privately built rocket launched from Indian soil.

The flight is the first of three planned developmental missions before Vikram-1 enters commercial service, targeting the growing global market for dedicated and rideshare launches of small satellites used in Earth observation, communications, and scientific research.

What This Means for India's Space Sector

Until Friday, every satellite launch from Indian soil had been carried out exclusively by the Indian Space Research Organisation. The success of Vikram-1 marks a concrete step in India's space sector reforms, under which private companies are now permitted to develop and operate orbital launch vehicles.

For India's diaspora — many of whom work in the global aerospace and technology sectors — the launch signals that Indian startups can build reliable launch vehicles and compete with established private space companies from the United States and Europe. The small-satellite launch market, currently constrained on the supply side, represents a significant commercial opportunity that Skyroot is positioning to capture.

Former ISRO Chairman S. Somanath extended his best wishes ahead of the launch, describing the mission as a significant milestone for India's private space ecosystem. With Vikram-1's success now confirmed, the next chapter for Indian private spaceflight is no longer a matter of aspiration — it has arrived.
